instruction: Judge whether the rewrite preserves all substantive reasoning of the original, without omissions, unsupported additions or changes in actor, mechanism, condition, timing, scope, direction or effect. Use preserved only if all survive, changed for a material difference, uncertain if unresolved. Give specific evidence. Independently map each supplied original source passage index to the closest corresponding exact contiguous quotation in the rewrite; use null if absent. A quote can identify a changed relation; it is not a vote that the relation was preserved. Quotes are for analysis only.

Give the mower crew a few minutes for a line sweep before each cut. Loose kite string is hard to see in the grass and can wind around a mower spindle. Everyone tends to launch from the same bare patch. Moving the launch flags a little each week gives the grass time to grow back. Children like to watch from directly under the kites. A bench with a good view off to one side gives families a comfortable spot clear of the lines.

People taking a shortcut across the grass may never notice a line stretched in front of them. A mown path around the edge gives walkers an obvious way through. One school outing can fill the whole field. Listing group visits on the noticeboard lets regular flyers choose a quieter time. Wind often scatters tiny clips during assembly. A shallow lipped tray on the work table keeps the fittings together until the kite is ready.
documents.rewrite:
Allow the mowing crew a few minutes before every cut to look for stray kite string. It's easy to miss among the grass blades, where it can wrap around a mower spindle. Since flyers tend to start from the same worn patch, shift the launch flags a short distance each week to let the grass recover. Children often want to watch from right underneath the kites. Put a bench off to one side where families can sit comfortably, enjoy the view and stay clear of the lines.

Mow a path along the perimeter so walkers have an obvious route across the field. Anyone cutting over the grass could walk straight into a stretched line without seeing it. Post group visits on the noticeboard so regular flyers can come at a quieter hour, since a single school outing can take up the entire field. For kite assembly, put a shallow tray with a rim on the work table. The wind often carries off the little clips, and the rim will keep the fittings in one place until the kite is ready.

A quartet can set up much faster if it knows what is already in the room. Put a dated equipment list beside the booking form so players can decide what to bring. Some players arrive after everyone else has begun. Giving them the door code in the booking message saves the ensemble from stopping mid-piece to let them in. Put a pencil groove or clip on each music stand. Players mark bowings as they rehearse, and a pencil that stays on the stand is always within reach.

A drum kit can drown a flute in a small room. Stock a set of practice pads so mixed groups can hear the quieter parts while they work through a passage. A photo of the mixer's usual settings gives the next ensemble a quick starting point after a group has turned individual channels up or down. Leave the piano tuner's visit on the shared calendar. Ensembles scheduling a recording can pick a date when the instrument will have just been tuned.
documents.rewrite:

Include the door code in the booking message so anyone arriving after rehearsal has begun can come in without interrupting a piece. Give every music stand a groove or clip for a pencil so players always have one to hand when they want to mark a bowing during rehearsal.

In a small room the drums can easily overpower a flute. Keep practice pads on hand so a mixed ensemble working through a passage can hear the softer parts. Take a photo of the usual mixer settings. If one ensemble changes the levels on individual channels, the next can use the photo to get started quickly. Keep the piano tuner's appointment on the shared calendar so a group booking a recording can choose a day just after the tuning.

Ask residents to mark a small box on the signup slip if they prefer a doorstep copy. People who rarely get to the shops would still receive the bulletin. Arrange a delivery time with each shopkeeper. A bundle arriving before the doors open otherwise has to travel around the route a second time. Give readers a phone number for address changes. Someone who moves within the neighborhood can keep receiving a copy, and the old doorstep stops accumulating papers.

A full rack by the checkout is easy to overlook among the sale leaflets. A small sign above it telling shoppers the bulletin is free gives them a reason to take one. A holiday street closure can cut a carrier off halfway around the block. Note announced closures on the week's route map so the carrier can enter from the other end. Let households pause a doorstep delivery for a specified week. They can go away without coming back to a pile of old bulletins.
documents.rewrite:
Put a small checkbox on the signup slip and ask residents to tick it if they'd like the bulletin delivered to their door. That reaches people who seldom make it to the shops. Agree on a delivery time with each shopkeeper so the carrier doesn't arrive before opening and have to take the bundle around the route again. Give readers a number to call when they change address. If they move elsewhere in the neighborhood, their copies can follow them and papers won't pile up at the old door.

Even a full rack by the checkout can get lost among the sale leaflets. Put a small sign above it inviting shoppers to take a free bulletin. Mark announced closures on the carrier's map for that week. If a street closes for a holiday and cuts off the route halfway around a block, the carrier can get in from the opposite end. Let a household name the week it wants doorstep delivery put on hold so it can go away and return to a clear doorstep.

Make a few large loop handles for children who find a narrow stick difficult to hold. They can move their own characters without an adult taking over. Give the youngest audience members cushions on the floor at the front. They can see the whole screen without having to look around adult shoulders. Some children dislike a room going dark all at once. Dim the lights in stages and tell them when the show is about to start so they can settle in.

Leave a clear approach to one side of the screen at seated height. A child using a wheelchair can bring a puppet into the same scene as a standing partner. Children behind the sheet can't see the faces out front. Let pairs trade places after each short scene so they can see how their work looks from the audience. Set out a small sample of colored translucent paper beside the silhouettes. Children can hold it up to the light and choose a color that actually shows on the screen.
documents.rewrite:
Fit a few puppets with large loop handles. Children who struggle to grip a thin stick can then move their own characters without an adult having to do it for them. Lay cushions on the floor in front for the youngest spectators, where they'll have the whole screen in view without adult shoulders in the way. Tell the children when the show is about to begin and lower the lights a little at a time. That gives anyone who dislikes sudden darkness a chance to settle.

Keep the way clear to one side of the screen and make sure a child can reach it from a seated position. A child in a wheelchair can then play a puppet in the same scene as a partner who's standing. From behind the sheet the children can't see the audience's faces. Have partners swap sides after each short scene so both get to see what their work looks like from the seats. Beside the silhouettes, set out a small selection of translucent colored paper for children to hold to the light and pick a color that will show up on the screen.

A row of card stacks hides most of the pictures. Prop up one of each design so visitors can pick out a view they recognize. Postage depends on where the card is going, so have the stamp volunteer ask the destination before handing over a stamp. That keeps a card for overseas from leaving with domestic postage. A child may have a whole story to send before they can form the letters. A volunteer who takes dictation can get the child's own words onto the card.

Keep a few card designs in reserve for the afternoon so late arrivals still have a choice of pictures. A short ruler makes a good line guide on the blank side. Writers can move it down as they go and keep their lines from drifting into each other. Name a volunteer to take the collection box to the post office at closing. Cards left in the final few minutes then have someone responsible for getting them into the mail.
documents.rewrite:
Stand one card of each design upright. A row of stacks conceals most of the pictures, and seeing them all makes it easier for a visitor to choose a familiar view. Have the volunteer issuing stamps ask where each card is headed before giving the writer a stamp. The destination determines the postage, and an overseas card could otherwise go out with a domestic stamp. Some children have a whole story to tell before they've learned to write the letters. A volunteer can take dictation so the words on the card are the child's own.

Set aside a few designs for the afternoon to give people who arrive late a choice of pictures. Provide a short ruler for the blank side of the card. Writers can slide it down a line at a time to keep one line of writing from running into the next. Choose a volunteer to carry the collection box to the post office at closing so someone is responsible for mailing even the cards slipped in during the last few minutes.

A Saturday return still has to go through the wash. Block out drying and folding time on the booking calendar so Sunday's group is offered only what can be ready. A washable hall mark in one corner helps a caterer sort the hall's cloths from their own when both sets turn up in the same laundry load. A booking for forty guests can grow after invitations go out. Set a date for the borrower to confirm the final quantity while staff still have time to adjust the order.

A stack can look spotless while a mark hides inside a fold. Open each tablecloth under a bright light before packing it so the borrower gets a presentable set. Put a picture of the collection door in the pickup email. First-time borrowers can go straight to the linen room even when the main hall is locked. When a group's tables have different shapes, pack by room and table number. Its setup crew can take each bundle straight to the right spot.
documents.rewrite:
When linens come back on Saturday, they still need washing. Reserve time on the booking calendar to dry and fold them so staff offer Sunday's group only what they can have ready. Mark one corner of each cloth with a washable hall identifier. Then a caterer who finds the hall's linens mixed with their own in one wash can sort them out. A group expecting forty may grow once the invitations go out. Give the borrower a date to confirm how many cloths they need, early enough for staff to revise the order.

Even a clean-looking stack can conceal a stain in a fold. Unfold every cloth in bright light before packing to ensure the borrower receives a presentable set. Include a photo of the collection door in the pickup email so someone borrowing for the first time can go directly to the linen room even if the main hall is locked. For a group using tables of several shapes, make up the bundles by room and table number so the setup crew can carry each one directly to its place.

Walk the route at the planned hour a few days ahead. A fountain or a delivery truck that runs every morning might otherwise drown out the first stop. A clock-face direction such as “two o'clock from the gate” gives everyone the same reference point when the singer is hidden in leaves. Choose a stop with a bench for the longest listening spell. Walkers who need a seat can stay for the whole discussion.

The group may stretch out on a narrow path. Ask someone familiar with the route to walk last so a person who pauses to listen can find their way back to the others. If a likely identification divides the group, write down the phrase and the competing guesses. Walkers can check the same evidence against recordings afterward. Keep ringtones off during listening stops. An electronic chirp from a pocket can sound remarkably like another bird joining in.
documents.rewrite:
Try the route a few days beforehand at the hour you plan to hold the walk. A fountain or a truck making its morning delivery might drown out the birds at your first stop. When a bird is singing from the cover of leaves, give a clock-face direction from a landmark everyone can use, such as “two o'clock from the gate.” Plan the longest stretch of listening at a bench so anyone who needs to sit can stay for the entire discussion.

On a narrow path people can end up quite far apart. Have someone who knows the route bring up the rear so a walker who stops to listen can find the others again. When people disagree about a likely identification, note the song phrase they heard along with the different guesses. After the walk they can all compare that same evidence with recordings. Ask walkers to silence their ringtones at listening stops, since a phone chirping in someone's pocket can sound like a second bird joining the first.

Someone choosing a pen for a daily planner needs to know how it behaves on those pages. Leave room for them to try a few words in their own planner as well. Arrange the pens in shallow grooved trays. A visitor can set one down to inspect the writing without having it roll onto the floor. A fountain pen can make a line under its own weight. Demonstrate that on a scrap before handing it over so a newcomer can start without bearing down on the nib.

A couple of ordinary loops can feel comfortable even with a pen that's tiring over time. Offer enough space to write a full paragraph and judge the grip. Seat a left-handed writer at the left end of a shared table when they prefer it. Their elbow then has room to move through a line. Show which pens the owners are happy to have used with the cap on the back. Visitors can explore how the extra weight feels without guessing what a borrowed pen will tolerate.
documents.rewrite:
Make space for people shopping for a daily planner pen to write a few words in their own planners too. They'll want to see how the pen writes on the pages they'll actually use. Lay the pens out in shallow trays with grooves so a visitor can put one down to look at the writing without the pen rolling to the floor. Before handing a fountain pen to a first-time user, show on a scrap how it draws a line under its own weight. They can start writing with a light touch on the nib.

Give people enough writing space to try a whole paragraph. A couple of simple loops might feel fine even if the grip becomes tiring with longer use. If a left-handed writer prefers the left end of a shared table, seat them there so their elbow has room to move as they write across the line. Point out which owners are comfortable having the cap slipped onto the back of their pen. Visitors can feel what the added weight does without having to guess whether a borrowed pen can take it.
